issues.legal_issue: A compensation determination for an original plot not allotted in the final scheme is not appealable as an estimate of increment.
material_facts: The landholder's original plot was taken for the town-planning scheme, and no plot was allotted to him in the final scheme.
He challenged the compensation determination, arguing that it was appealable as a decision estimating increment.
Increment under the Act compared the value of the same final plot with and without the contemplated improvements; it did not determine the value of the original plot.
issues.conclusion: The compensation determination did not fall within the appealable category concerning estimation of increment.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 32(1)(viii) and 34 of the Bombay Town Planning Act, 1954, an appeal lies from a decision estimating increment under section 65. Increment is the difference between the market value of the same final plot with and without contemplated improvements, assessed at the date of the declaration of intention to make the scheme. Rule 17(v) of the Bombay Town Planning Rules, 1955, and Form B distinguish the valuation of the final plot from that of the original plot. The value of an original plot therefore does not arise under the increment-estimation clause.

predicates.town_planning_compensation_appeal: A person appealed a town-planning officer's determination of compensation.
predicates.owner_received_no_reconstituted_plot: The original-plot owner was not allotted a reconstituted plot in the final scheme.
predicates.challenged_compensation_concerns_origina: The challenged compensation determination concerned the value of the owner's original plot rather than the increment in the value of a final plot.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges compensation concerning an original plot that was not reconstituted in the final scheme, the determination is not appealable as an increment estimate.

issues.legal_issue: Taking land for a town-planning scheme does not, by itself, amount to injurious affection of that acquired land.
material_facts: The landholder's plot was taken for the purposes of the scheme, and he was not allotted a plot in the final scheme.
He sought compensation for the loss of the land and argued that the decision was appealable as an estimate of compensation for property or rights injuriously affected.
The property for which compensation was claimed was the land acquired for the scheme.
issues.conclusion: The acquired land itself was not property injuriously affected within the meaning of the provision, so the compensation determination did not fall within the appealable category for injurious affection.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 32(1)(xiii), 34 and 69 of the Bombay Town Planning Act, 1954, concern compensation for property or rights injuriously affected by a scheme. The affected property or right must be other than that acquired for the scheme and must remain with its owner. The Court applied the generally accepted meaning of “injurious affection” reflected in section 23(1), fourthly, of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, which concerns damage to other property of the person interested. The Court found no basis for construing the expression differently in the town-planning statute.

predicates.town_planning_compensation_appeal: A person appealed a town-planning officer's determination of compensation.
predicates.land_taken_for_scheme: The land in respect of which compensation was claimed was taken for the purposes of the town-planning scheme.
predicates.claimed_injury_is_to_acquired_land: The claimed injury concerned the acquired land itself, rather than other property or a right retained by the owner.

issues.definition: When the appeal concerns injury claimed only to land taken for the scheme, that land is not treated as retained property injuriously affected for this compensation appeal category.

issues.legal_issue: An owner whose original plot is not allotted in the final scheme remains entitled to compensation assessed by reference to the original plot's market value.
material_facts: The landholder owned an original plot that was taken for the scheme and was not allotted a plot in the final scheme.
The landholder disputed the compensation determined for the loss of that land.
The Act provided for payment of the net loss to an owner not given a plot in the final scheme and used the original plots' market values in calculating the relevant difference.
issues.conclusion: The Act provided a mechanism to compensate an owner not allotted a reconstituted plot; compensation was assessed by reference to the market value of the original plot at the date of the declaration of intention to make the scheme.
issues.legal_principle: Section 71 of the Bombay Town Planning Act, 1954, provides for payment of an owner's net loss when the owner of an original plot is not provided with a plot in the final scheme. The governing valuation date is the date of the declaration of intention to make the scheme. In determining the difference under section 32(1)(iii), the Town Planning Officer uses the market value of each original plot as specified in section 64(1)(f). In State of Gujarat v. Shantilal Mangaldas, the Court explained that the Act adjusts compensation for loss of land against contributions to the scheme and applies the same compensation principle whether or not an owner receives a reconstituted plot.

issues.definition: In a town-planning scheme, an owner of an original plot who receives no reconstituted plot is entitled to compensation for the resulting net loss.
